roles.why: The exterior and interior three-point couplings are the same real coefficient.
Orthogonal projectors exist and the state expansion converges.

steps.slogan: Resolve the intermediate radial state into conformal multiplets.
steps.detail: For each primary multiplet, form its orthogonal projector using an orthonormal descendant basis. Completeness makes the identity equal to the sum of these projectors, with null states removed. A scalar pair on an axis is invariant under its O(d-1) stabilizer. Its matrix elements on rotated axes are functions on the sphere. The Peter-Weyl decomposition of these functions consists of spherical harmonics, whose tensor representatives are symmetric traceless tensors. Thus only these spin representations can have a nonzero scalar-pair overlap.

steps.slogan: Insert each projector between the two scalar pairs.
steps.detail: The resulting matrix element is the exchange of one multiplet. Its position dependence is the conformal block, while the two three-point couplings multiply. Reality and the orthonormal primary convention make this product $f_{\phi\phi O}^2$.

steps.slogan: Use Bose symmetry and positivity to restrict the exchanges.
steps.detail: The scalar-scalar-spin numerator changes by $(-1)^\ell$ under exchange of the equal scalars. Hence odd-spin couplings vanish. Every remaining real coefficient has nonnegative square. Pairing the convergent projector sum gives the full expansion.

roles.why: The central quadratic Casimir has the same eigenvalue on all descendants.
Their differential conformal action gives the pair Casimir without spin terms.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the central Casimir on the primary.
steps.detail: Write the Casimir in dilation, translation, special conformal, and rotation generators. The primary conditions $K|O\rangle=0$ and $D|O\rangle=\Delta|O\rangle$ reduce its eigenvalue to $\Delta(\Delta-d)+\ell(\ell+d-2)$. Centrality gives the same value on descendants.

steps.slogan: Move the pair Casimir through the multiplet projector.
steps.detail: The projector onto an irreducible multiplet commutes with conformal generators. Acting with the Casimir on the state from the first scalar pair is therefore equivalent to its eigenvalue acting on the projected exchange.

steps.slogan: Convert the pair action to a differential equation.
steps.detail: Each conformal generator acts on the two external scalar positions by its primary differential operator. Sum the two actions, square to form the pair Casimir, then remove the usual four-point prefactor. The resulting operator $\mathcal D$ acts only on $u,v$ and has the stated eigenvalue on the block.

roles.why: The two commuting global $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ factors separate the Casimir equation.
The branch and leading powers select the conformal block rather than its shadow.

steps.slogan: Separate the two global conformal Casimir equations.
steps.detail: In two dimensions, the holomorphic and antiholomorphic global algebras commute. A primary has weights $h=(\Delta+\ell)/2$ and $\bar h=(\Delta-\ell)/2$, so its block is a product of two one-variable eigenfunctions.

steps.slogan: Solve the one-variable equation with the primary boundary condition.
steps.detail: The equation $[t^2(1-t)\partial_t^2-t^2\partial_t]k_{2h}=h(h-1)k_{2h}$ becomes the hypergeometric equation after $k_{2h}=t^hF(t)$. The solution analytic at zero with $F(0)=1$ is ${}_2F_1(h,h;2h;t)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two orientations of the spin representation.
steps.detail: Multiply the holomorphic solution by the antiholomorphic solution, then add the term with $h,\bar h$ exchanged. This gives the stated symmetrized normalization. At spin zero the formula contains two identical terms. Divide by 2 if a unit leading scalar block is desired; it is not a Virasoro block.

roles.why: These quantum numbers fix the two holomorphic parameters in the Casimir solution.

steps.slogan: Build an antisymmetric product of one-variable Casimir solutions.
steps.detail: The cited derivation uses $k_a(z)k_b(\bar z)-k_b(z)k_a(\bar z)$, where $a=\Delta+\ell$ and $b=\Delta-\ell-2$. Both factors solve their hypergeometric differential equations.

steps.slogan: Insert the product into the four-dimensional Casimir operator.
steps.detail: The cited calculation multiplies the antisymmetric product by $z\bar z/(z-\bar z)$. Substitution into equation (165) uses the two one-variable equations to cancel mixed derivative terms. The remaining eigenvalue is $\Delta(\Delta-4)+\ell(\ell+2)$. The cited published proof uses the intertwiner $D_2(x-z)^{-1}=(x-z)^{-1}(D_0|_{a\mapsto a-1,b\mapsto b-1,c\mapsto c-2}-c+2)$, equation (2.10). Its separated hypergeometric eigenfunctions give equation (2.11) with $\lambda_1=(\Delta+\ell)/2$ and $\lambda_2=(\Delta-\ell)/2$.

steps.slogan: Fix the OPE branch and extend across equal cross-ratios.
steps.detail: The small-$z,\bar z$ primary asymptotics fix the normalization in equation (167). Antisymmetry makes the numerator vanish at $z=\bar z$, so the apparent denominator singularity is removable at regular points. This is an outline of the published differential calculation, not a local formal check. The source boundary condition takes z to zero first and then x to zero, with leading power $x^{\lambda_1}z^{\lambda_2}$. The regular primary branch and this leading coefficient determine the solution; the displayed factor $(-1)^\ell/2^\ell$ is the scalar-block normalization of the cited lecture formula.

statement: For identical real scalar pairs in a unitary [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) with $d>2$, a conformal block in [radial](c:qft-radial-quantization) coordinates has [correlation function](c:correlation-function) expansion $g_{\Delta,\ell}=\sum_{n,j}B_{n,j}r^{\Delta+n}C_j^{(d-2)/2}(\cos\theta)$ with $B_{n,j}\geq0$ in the positive Gegenbauer normalization, for $r<1$.

hypotheses.text: The external pair is identical and real, and the radial representation is unitary. The Euclidean dimension is at least 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.

The two scalar pairs have radial separation $r<1$, and the descendant energy-spin basis is complete. Both identical pairs use opposite points at equal radius in the symmetric rho frame, and r is the absolute rho coordinate.

roles.why: Pair overlaps multiply with their conjugates and are nonnegative squared norms.
The positive radial evolution time gives a convergent spectral decomposition.

steps.slogan: Insert orthogonal energy and spin projectors in the block.
steps.detail: Write the exchange as a matrix element of $e^{-\tau D}$ with $r=e^{-\tau}$. A level-$n$ descendant has energy $\Delta+n$, so its contribution contains $r^{\Delta+n}$.

steps.slogan: Use rotational covariance to contract the spin tensors.
steps.detail: The overlap of a scalar pair on an axis $n$ with a spin-$j$ state is proportional to the traceless tensor power of $n$. Contract it with the overlap on axis $n'$ to obtain a positive normalization constant times $C_j^{(d-2)/2}(n\cdot n')$.

steps.slogan: Collect the nonnegative spectral weights for each level and spin.
steps.detail: Reality and radial adjoints make the remaining weight the sum of absolute squares of the overlap coefficients. Hence $B_{n,j}\geq0$. The identity of the two scalar insertions removes odd angular spin. At zero angle, positive Gegenbauer values also make each energy contribution nonnegative. In this symmetric frame, reversal of the axis exchanges the two identical insertions at the same radius and leaves the pair state fixed. An odd spherical harmonic changes sign under this reversal, so its overlap vanishes.

steps.slogan: Isolate the identity contribution in the crossing equation.
steps.detail: Normalize the scalar two-point function to one, so its identity OPE coefficient is one. Move no terms across the equation. The relation then reads $F_1+\sum_Op_OF_O=0$, with $p_O=f_{\phi\phi O}^2\geq0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the functional to the full convergent relation.
steps.detail: Linearity and the stated interchange condition give $\alpha(F_1)+\sum_Op_O\alpha(F_O)=0$. Every term in the sum is nonnegative under the proposed spectrum.

steps.slogan: Compare strict positivity with the zero crossing value.
steps.detail: The identity term is strictly positive. Adding the nonnegative exchange terms gives a strictly positive left side, which cannot equal zero. Thus no conformal data with that spectrum can obey both unitarity and crossing. A finite numerical sample alone does not establish positivity over the full allowed spectrum.

roles.why: Its direct-channel correlator tends to one while the crossing prefactor tends to zero.
A finite set of regular global blocks has at most logarithmic powers in the crossed diagonal limit.

steps.slogan: Take the direct-channel short-distance limit.
steps.detail: Set $z=\bar z=t$ and let $t\downarrow0$. The identity contributes one. Every other global primary has positive dimension and its direct-channel block vanishes, so a finite proposed expansion tends to one.

steps.slogan: Estimate each block in the crossed channel.
steps.detail: A global factor $k_{2h}(1-t)$ is bounded by a constant times $1+|\log t|$ for regular positive $h$, from the zero-balanced hypergeometric equation. A weight-zero chiral factor is constant by its regular limit. Each two-dimensional global block is therefore at most of order $(1+|\log t|)^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare a finite crossed sum with the identity limit.
steps.detail: Crossing multiplies the crossed sum by $(t/(1-t))^{2\Delta_\phi}$. Since $\Delta_\phi>0$, this factor times any fixed logarithmic square tends to zero. A finite sum would make the same correlator tend both to zero and to one, a contradiction. The theorem counts global primaries, not Virasoro primaries.
